source: Satopaa and Ungar (2015) Combining and Extremizing Real-Valued Forecasts
finding: A weighted average of forecasts is never fully efficient. It behaves as if it holds less information than the forecasters together hold, so it needs to be pushed away from the mean.
numbers: Theory plus simulated data and a real data set (UCI, 8 predictors, two models). Real data fitted extremizing slope: 1.695 with no information overlap, 1.438 with high overlap. Quadratic loss: extremized combination 155.69 vs 185.74 for the best single model M2 (no overlap; lower is better).
quote: extremizing is likely to be more beneficial under no or low information overlap
limits: Linear extremizing only. Needs a training set with known outcomes. Authors say extremizing is 'probably not' guaranteed to help and is likelier to help with low information overlap.
agent_relevance: Extremizing is a fix for independent partial information. Samples from one model share information, so the fitted slope should be near 1 (G4).

source: Satopaa and Ungar (2015) Combining and Extremizing Real-Valued Forecasts (discussion section)
finding: Extremizing matters more when forecasters' combined information grows and when their information sets are more diverse. Close collaborators need little extremizing; widely different sources need heavy extremizing.
numbers: Qualitative conclusion, citing Satopaa et al. (2015b) Gaussian partial-information fits.
limits: Stated as a pattern from a Gaussian model, not a controlled experiment on people.
agent_relevance: Our samples are the close-collaborator case at the limit (same weights, same prompt). Extremizing should be zero or small.

source: Satopaa, Pemantle, Ungar (2015) Modeling Probability Forecasts via Information Diversity
finding: A partial-overlap information model gives the optimal amount of extremizing as a function of overlap. The oracle aggregate is more likely to be more extreme than the probit average, which the authors say explains why extremizing is 'almost certainly called for' for diverse forecasters.
numbers: Good Judgment Project super-forecasters, year 2: 44 forecasters, 123 events (23 occurred), 17-34 forecasts per event (mean 24.2). Mean Brier: arithmetic mean 0.132; log-odds 0.128; probit 0.128; revealed aggregator (extremizing by overlap model) 0.123. Reliability 0.026 -> 0.020; resolution 0.045 -> 0.049; uncertainty 0.152.
quote: Overall, p-bar presents the worst performance.
limits: One small data set, super-forecasters only, one event at a time with no training set. The gain is 0.009 Brier. Authors call it a first attempt.
agent_relevance: A modest, real gain for independent human experts. About 7% is a realistic ceiling even when extremizing is justified.

source: Satopaa, Jensen, Mellers, Tetlock, Ungar (2014) Probability aggregation in time-series (Annals of Applied Statistics 8(2))
finding: On IARPA tournament data, models that calibrate the aggregate beat a smoothing-only model and plain exponentially weighted averages. The sharpest variant (BSACLOG) is overconfident and has high variance. The smoothing model is underconfident because the experts are underconfident as a group.
numbers: Over 2300 experts, 166 events, 17,475 daily Brier scores, 10-fold CV. Overall by day: SACLOG 0.096; SACBRI 0.096; BSACLOG 0.097; SDLM 0.100; EWMLA 0.102; EWMBA 0.104; EWMA 0.111 (worst).
quote: overconfidence can pay off frequently enough to compensate for a few large losses
limits: BSACLOG wins on short easy questions only; there overconfidence pays often enough to cover a few large losses. Longer questions punish it.
agent_relevance: Sharpening helps when inputs are under-confident as a group. Overshooting gives rare large losses; any push in the scaffold should be capped.

source: Satopaa (2018) Combining Information from Multiple Forecasters: Inefficiency of Central Tendency
finding: Any aggregator that stays strictly between the smallest and largest forecast (mean, median, trimmed mean, midrange) is never efficient when forecasters use different information. Even with zero-centred noise it is asymptotically inefficient.
numbers: Theorems. Applied note: on geopolitical questions the equally weighted mean was under-confident, and moving it directly away from 0.5 significantly cut squared error (citing Baron et al. 2014 and Satopaa et al. 2014).
limits: Assumes forecasters use their information accurately. If they are noisy copies of one signal, central tendency can be fine.
agent_relevance: Median and mean are right for noisy copies of the same signal. The inefficiency result needs distinct information, which parallel samples lack.

source: Neyman and Roughgarden (2022) Are You Smarter Than a Random Expert? The Robust Aggregation of Substitutable Signals
finding: Under a worst-case but 'substitutable signals' condition, averaging beats trusting a random expert. With a known prior, averaging then extremizing by a constant factor gives a better guarantee. No fixed factor is best on both fully correlated and fully independent signals.
numbers: Two experts: tight approximation ratio 0.706 ((3+sqrt7)/8) without prior; 0.760 with prior and extremizing. For k experts: extremizing reaches about 2.598/k; best possible with a fixed factor is 4k/(k+1)^2. Suggested factor rises with k but is capped near sqrt(3)=1.732.
quote: In the first case, it is optimal not to extremize; in the second, it is optimal to extremize a lot.
limits: Worst-case theory, not data. Needs the projective-substitutes assumption and a known prior.
agent_relevance: The worst-case-safe factor is small (under 1.73) because the aggregator cannot tell correlated from independent signals. Our agent cannot tell either, so a large factor is unsafe (G4).

source: Neyman (2024) Algorithmic Bayesian Epistemology (thesis), sections 2.2.2 and 7.5
finding: Worked example: two experts both say 2/3. If they saw the same coin flip, the right answer is 2/3. If they saw different independent flips, the right answer is 3/4. Averaging is right in the first case and too timid in the second. Log-pool then extremize is called a state-of-the-art method.
numbers: Coin example: shared evidence -> 2/3; independent evidence -> 3/4. Theorem 7.5.1 factor stays under sqrt(3) as k grows; said to be consistent with Satopaa (2022) and Satopaa and Ungar (2015).
limits: Secondary synthesis by the author of the theorems. Empirical support cited, not re-run.
agent_relevance: A clean test for G4: extremize only if samples saw different evidence. Resampling one model sees the same evidence.

source: Halawi, Zhang, Yueh-Han, Steinhardt (2024) Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models
finding: A retrieval plus fine-tuned reasoning system ensembles 6 forecasts with a trimmed mean. Averaging the system with the crowd beats both. The system hedges toward 0.5 and rarely outputs low probabilities.
numbers: Test set (914 questions, 5 platforms, after June 2023): system 0.179 vs crowd 0.149 Brier; system+crowd weighted average (4x crowd) 0.146; random 0.250. Crowd uncertain (0.3-0.7): system 0.199 vs crowd 0.246. Crowd near 0 or 1: system accuracy 7% higher but Brier 0.04 worse.
quote: our model hedges, even as the evidence
limits: The system still loses overall. Hedging is blamed on safety training; no extremizing arm was tested.
agent_relevance: Models hedge, so a push away from 0.5 might help at the extremes. But a push must not be applied where the crowd is uncertain, where the system did best.

source: Halawi et al. (2024) Appendix: ensembling methods on validation set
finding: Five ensemble methods were compared; trimmed mean was chosen. A language-model consensus step (universal self-consistency) was worse than no ensemble.
numbers: Validation Brier: USC 0.1691 vs no-ensemble 0.1676 (worse); mean 0.1656; median 0.1651; geometric mean 0.1655; trimmed mean 0.1649; human crowd 0.1600.
limits: Only 6 members per question. Differences among numeric aggregators are 0.0007 or less.
agent_relevance: Aggregate numbers, not prose. The choice among numeric aggregators matters little.

source: Karger et al. (2025) ForecastBench: A Dynamic Benchmark of AI Forecasting Capabilities
finding: An LLM ensemble of 3 models x 3 superforecaster prompts (9 forecasts per question) was built with median, geometric mean and geometric mean of log odds. Geometric forms were best by a small margin. No extremizing arm.
numbers: Table 17 Brier: median 0.197 (2SE 0.024); trimmed mean 0.197; geometric mean 0.194; geometric mean of log odds 0.194. Superforecasters 0.096, general public 0.121, best LLM (Claude 3.5 Sonnet) 0.122 on the 200-item subset.
limits: Aggregator differences (0.003) are far inside the standard error (0.024). Question sets differ across papers.
agent_relevance: Log-odds averaging is a safe default; the benchmark team did not try extremizing.

source: Schoenegger, Tuminauskaite, Park, Tetlock (2024) Wisdom of the Silicon Crowd (Study 1)
finding: Median of 12 LLMs on 31 binary questions was not different from 925 human forecasters, and beat a 50% baseline. Models showed acquiescence bias: mean predictions above 50% although resolutions were nearly even. The median aggregate offset it.
numbers: LLM crowd Brier 0.20 (SD 0.12) vs 0.25 baseline: t(30)=-2.35, p=0.026. LLM crowd vs human crowd 0.19 (SD 0.19): t(60)=0.19, p=0.850. Equivalence bounds d=0.5 (0.081 Brier): both one-sided tests p<0.05. Single models: GPT-4 0.15, Claude 2 0.21, Coral 0.38.
limits: Only 31 questions; wide equivalence bounds. Single GPT-4 (0.15) beat the ensemble median (0.20), so the ensemble did not beat its best member.
agent_relevance: Median over different models helps; this is not evidence that many samples of one model help. The bias is directional (yes-leaning), so pushing outward would amplify it.

source: Schoenegger et al. (2024) Study 2: exposing LLMs to the human median
finding: Showing GPT-4 and Claude 2 the human crowd median and asking them to update raised accuracy, but a plain average of human and machine forecasts beat that.
numbers: Accuracy improved by between 17% and 28% after exposure to the human median; simple human-machine averaging was better.
limits: Two models, small question set.
agent_relevance: Averaging independent sources beats asking a model to reconcile them in prose.

source: Hsieh, Fu, Chen et al. (2024) Reasoning and Tools for Human-Level Forecasting
finding: Ensembles of ReAct tool-using agents beat single agents, but ensembles of plain base models did not help. Ensembling only helps if members are already calibrated.
numbers: RTF ensemble median Brier 0.169 vs human crowd 0.172 (Manifold). Single agent 0.180 vs ensemble 0.169. Base GPT-4o ensemble 0.218 vs single 0.210 (worse). Ensemble std: base LM 0.150, ReAct 0.092.
quote: Ensembles only contribute to the final performance if each ensemble member is already sufficiently calibrated.
limits: Manifold questions only; ensembles of 3-4.
agent_relevance: More samples of an uncalibrated model do not fix it. Aggregation reduces variance, not bias.

source: Turtel et al. (2025) Outcome-based RL to Predict the Future
finding: A 7-run ensemble of an RL-tuned 14B model, using median prediction sampling, reaches 0.190 Brier on 1,265 held-out questions and improves calibration (ECE 0.062).
limits: The gain from ensembling alone is not isolated in this table. Still trails the market.
agent_relevance: Repeated samples of one tuned model with median gave a gain; no extremizing was tried.

source: Lu (2025) Evaluating LLMs on Real-World Forecasting Against Expert Forecasters
finding: Median and mean ensembles of repeated samples give almost identical Brier scores. Models are overconfident on events they think likely (Qwen-32B predicts near certainty for events that happen 50% of the time). Claude Sonnet with narrative prompts is underconfident (50% for 80% events).
numbers: Direct prediction median vs mean Brier: o3 0.1352 vs 0.1362; GPT-4.1 0.1542 vs 0.1509; Claude-3.5-Sonnet 0.1947 vs 0.1910; GPT-4o-mini 0.2743 vs 0.2676.
limits: Calibration direction depends on model and prompt, so one extremizing sign is wrong for some models.
agent_relevance: Extremizing would hurt overconfident models. Check the direction of miscalibration before any push.

source: Bench to the Future (2025) pastcasting benchmark
finding: All tested models and agents tend to predict Yes more often than outcomes warrant; calibration curves sit below the diagonal above 0.5.
numbers: Qualitative, from calibration plots for each model-agent pair.
limits: Pastcasting set; leakage risk.
agent_relevance: A Yes bias means pushing upward would add error, not remove it.

source: Berger, Analytis, Satopaa, Kurvers (2026) Beyond AI advice: independent aggregation boosts human-AI accuracy
finding: Keeping human and AI judgements independent and breaking ties with a second human beat AI-as-advisor on all 10 datasets.
numbers: 10 datasets (medical diagnostics, misinformation). Hybrid confirmation tree beat AI-as-advisor in all 10.
limits: Binary decisions, not probability forecasts; no extremizing.
agent_relevance: Independence is what makes aggregation work. Do not let one sample read another's answer before voting.

source: Turtel, Wilczewski, Skotheim, Satopaa, Tetlock (2026) How Proper Scoring Rules Shape LLM Forecasting
finding: Training LLM forecasters on five proper scoring rules gives models with similar aggregate scores but different bias, information and noise. Authors suggest combining models with different error profiles and learning an aggregation policy.
numbers: Brier-trained model best Brier and AUC; log-trained model best log score and lowest calibration error. No extremizing experiment.
limits: Ensemble design is only an idea for future work.
agent_relevance: Diversity of errors, not number of copies, is what aggregation needs.

source: Baron, Mellers, Tetlock, Stone, Ungar (2014) Two Reasons to Make Aggregated Probability Forecasts More Extreme, Decision Analysis
finding: Founding paper. Reason 1: each forecaster lacks information others have, so the average is too timid. Reason 2: forecasters tend to be individually under-confident and noisy, so their average sits too close to 0.5. Summary taken from how opened papers describe it.
numbers: Not opened (publisher returned 403). No numbers recorded.
limits: Open it before relying on any figure.
agent_relevance: Source of the 'missing information' justification, which needs independent information. G4 says our samples are not independent.

source: Satopaa, Baron, Foster, Mellers, Tetlock, Ungar (2014) Combining multiple probability predictions using a simple logit model, IJF
finding: Fits a logit-scale model with a bias-and-extremizing parameter on Good Judgment Project data. Described in opened papers as showing that extremizing helps.
numbers: Not opened (ScienceDirect 403). No numbers recorded.
limits: The fitted factor needed past outcomes.
agent_relevance: Base of the 'state of the art' claim; the factor was learned from past outcomes, which our scaffold lacks per task.

source: Mellers et al. (2014) Psychological strategies for winning a geopolitical forecasting tournament; Tetlock and Gardner (2015) Superforecasting
finding: Good Judgment Project won the IARPA tournament with teams, training, weighting and extremizing.
numbers: Not opened. No numbers recorded.
limits: The win mixes selection, training, teaming and extremizing, so extremizing alone is not isolated.
agent_relevance: Do not credit extremizing for the whole win.

source: Lichtendahl, Grushka-Cockayne, Jose, Winkler (2022) Extremizing and antiextremizing in Bayesian ensembles of binary-event forecasts, Operations Research
finding: Rival view. In a Bayesian ensemble model the right move can be to extremize or to anti-extremize (pull toward the middle), depending on dependence among forecasters. Known only from the title and reference list in Neyman 2024.
numbers: Not opened (publisher 403). No numbers recorded.
limits: Details unverified.
agent_relevance: If it holds, it supports G4: with dependent members the right adjustment may be a pull toward 0.5.

source: Palley and Soll (2019) Extracting the wisdom of crowds when information is shared, Management Science
finding: Shared information biases plain averages; collecting a second judgement from each person can help separate shared from private information.
numbers: Not opened; no numbers recorded.
limits: Details unverified; needs two judgements per person.
agent_relevance: A route to handle shared information without blind extremizing.

source: Sevilla (2021) Principled extremizing of aggregated forecasts
finding: Practitioner write-up of an extremizing formula for Metaculus-style forecasts; cited by Neyman 2024 as practical support.
numbers: Not opened (fetch failed). No numbers recorded.
limits: Blog source, unreviewed.
agent_relevance: Context only.

source: Halawi et al. (2024) Section 6.4 System complements the crowd
finding: Averaging an LLM system with the human crowd beat either alone in every setting tested. The best weight on the crowd was 4x.
numbers: Full test set Brier 0.149 (crowd) -> 0.146 (weighted average). Crowd between 0.3 and 0.7: crowd 0.24, system 0.237 when averaged unweighted; all-criteria row: system 0.240, crowd 0.247.
limits: Weight chosen on validation data. Gain is 0.003 on the full set.
agent_relevance: Mixing a diverse independent source with the model is worth more than reshaping one model's own samples.
